state.misconception_label: Does not understand that 2n represents an even number

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: Which of these shows part of the proof that the sum of two odd numbers is even? I got \( \begin{array}{l}2 n+(2 m+1) \\ =2(n+m)+1\end{array} \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have two containers, one with an odd number of marbles and another with another odd number of marbles. When you combine them, you can see that the total number of marbles is even. Just like when you add 2n and 2m+1 together to get 2(n+m)+1, which shows that the sum of two odd numbers is even.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Wait, but I'm confused... you said 2(n+m)+1 shows the sum is even, but doesn't that +1 at the end make it odd? Like, if I have an even number and add 1, that makes it odd, doesn't it?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of it like reading a number on a number line where each dash represents a different value. Just like how each dash on the number line is not always 2, adding 1 to an even number can still result in an even number. So, in the same way, adding 1 to the sum of two odd numbers can still give you an even number.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides mathematically incorrect information (claiming 2(n+m)+1 is even and that adding 1 to an even number can result in an even number), fails to address the student's core misconception about representing odd numbers as 2n+1, and the student's Turn 2 response shows they are more confused than at the start.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to use concrete analogies (marbles, number line), these analogies are either mathematically incorrect (Turn 1 gives an odd expression as proof of evenness, Turn 3 incorrectly claims adding 1 to an even number can be even) or confusing, failing to ground the abstract concept in accurate real-world reasoning.
